entry.title: LLMB: From Battery Papers to ML-Ready Databases

link.title: LLMB: From Battery Papers to ML-Ready Databases

entry.content:
ACS Central Science 2025

LLMB: Automated Battery Information Extraction and Database Construction Using Large Language Models

Combined LLM text mining with a graph digitizer in an agent pipeline to extract 8,074 cells of battery component + cyclability data from Li-MB literature at 96.4% accuracy — then connected it to ML capacity prediction.

What this paper does
An agent combining LLM-based text mining and a graph digitizer processes Li-MB literature to automatically extract battery material information. 29 entity categories. 8,074 cells. Component and cyclability database. 96.4% extraction accuracy. What's distinctive: the system also extracts data directly from cycling graphs embedded in papers — not just the prose. The resulting structured database is then fed directly into ML models for battery capacity prediction, closing the loop from text to numerical prediction.
Takeaway
◆ This paper connects what came before in this series: ML for battery data (Severson, Attia) and LLM for literature extraction (Dagdelen), merged into a single workflow — text extraction → structured database → ML prediction → experimental validation. That end-to-end integration is what makes it more than the sum of its parts. It's the direction I think the field is moving.
◇ The work ran almost simultaneously — and independently — with what I was building at SES AI. Different groups, same problem, similar intuition. When that happens, it usually means the need is real and the timing is right. The domain overlaps directly: LiMB, electrolyte, SEI — the same chemistry I spent my PhD studying experimentally, now being processed at scale by an LLM pipeline.
entry.summary: An LLM agent extracted 8,074 cells worth of battery data from Li-MB literature — including figures — at 96.4% accuracy, then connected it directly to ML capacity prediction.

entry.title: Structured Information Extraction from Materials Science Papers

link.title: Structured Information Extraction from Materials Science Papers

entry.content:
Nature Communications 2024 arxiv ↗

Structured information extraction from scientific text with large language models

Fine-tuned GPT-3 and Llama-2 to extract structured records — dopant-host links, MOF properties, composition/phase/application — from materials science text, outputting JSON at sentence and paragraph level.

What this paper does
Fine-tuned GPT-3 and Llama-2 on materials science literature to extract structured records from unstructured text. Three tasks were demonstrated: mapping dopant-host material relationships, cataloging metal-organic frameworks, and extracting composition/phase/morphology/application information. Processing happens at the sentence or paragraph level; output is JSON. Co-authors include Ceder, Persson, and Jain — the Materials Project team.
Takeaway
◆ The first paper to rigorously demonstrate "paper text → structured data via LLM" in materials chemistry. This overlaps most directly with what I built at SES AI — same direction, applied to battery electrolyte chemistry. The approach differed: they used fine-tuning; I used few-shot prompting with iterative domain-specific schema refinement. Their output was general entity-relations; mine targeted structured records directly usable for downstream model training. Same problem, different engineering choices — and a useful lens for explaining why those choices matter.
◇ The Materials Project co-authorship is not incidental. This is the same group that built the numerical database for inorganic materials — now extracting knowledge from text to complement it. The convergence of structured numerical data and structured textual knowledge is the long-term play.
entry.summary: Fine-tuned GPT-3 and Llama-2 to extract structured records from materials science text — demonstrating that LLMs can turn unstructured literature into queryable databases.

entry.title: What ML Can and Can’t Tell You About Batteries

link.title: What ML Can and Can’t Tell You About Batteries

entry.content:
Reflection 2025

What ML Can and Can't Tell You About Batteries

Severson predicts; Attia optimizes. But mechanistic understanding — the part that makes battery research actually progress — lives in the text of papers, not in cycling numbers. This is the structural gap pure data-driven approaches can't close.

What ML does well

Severson and Attia showed convincingly what’s possible: electrochemical time-series data can predict lifetime and guide protocol optimization. The loop of numerical data → pattern recognition → prediction or decision works, and it works well. These aren’t marginal improvements — 9.1% lifetime prediction error and 98% reduction in experimental time are real results.

The thing that keeps nagging me

Battery research — especially electrolyte design — is different from what those papers tackled. The question isn’t just “how long does this cell last?” It’s why it lasts that long. Why did this electrolyte form a stable SEI? How does the solvation shell structure influence the interphase? What does this particular additive actually do at the electrode surface?

During my PhD, I spent years on exactly these questions — XPS, Raman, NMR, post-mortem analysis, all trying to understand the mechanistic picture behind numbers that, on their face, just said “this one cycles better.” The answer to why almost always came from connecting your experimental results to what others had seen and proposed in the literature. The mechanistic insight was in the papers, not in the cycling data.

The structural problem with pure data-driven approaches

Battery ML faces a version of this problem systematically:

Three structural limitations
◆ Data scarcity. How many datasets exist with the same cell chemistry, cycling conditions, and characterization? The numerical data that battery ML trains on is fragmented across labs, formats, and conditions — nowhere near the scale of ImageNet or language data.
◇ Missing context. A voltage curve doesn't tell you what electrolyte was used, what the cell history was, or what degradation mechanism the authors suspected. That context exists — it's just in the paper text, not the numbers.
◇ Poor generalization. A model trained on LFP cells in one electrolyte system doesn't transfer cleanly to NMC cells in another. The mechanistic assumptions are different. Without those assumptions made explicit, the model is brittle.

All of this context — decades of experimental results, mechanistic interpretations, failure mode analyses — is accumulated in the scientific literature. ML, as practiced in Severson and Attia, doesn’t read it.

The shift: LLM as the missing piece

LLMs changed this. For the first time, it became possible to systematically extract structured knowledge from paper text at scale — not just keyword search, but genuine information extraction: what electrolyte, what additive, what SEI composition, what cycling performance, what mechanism was proposed.

The combination I think matters is: numerical data for finding patterns, text data for understanding what those patterns mean. When those two are connected, data-driven materials science can do something it couldn’t before — not just predict from numbers, but reason from the accumulated knowledge of a field.

The next two posts are about papers that started building exactly that.
entry.summary: ML predicts and optimizes. But the mechanistic understanding that makes battery research actually work lives in text — and that's a structural gap pure data-driven approaches can't close.

entry.title: Closed-Loop Optimization of Fast-Charging Protocols
entry.content:
Nature 2020 paper ↗

Closed-loop optimization of fast-charging protocols for batteries with machine learning

Extended Severson's prediction framework into closed-loop optimization: Bayesian optimization autonomously iterated experiment design → test → feedback to find high-performance fast-charging protocols, cutting experimental time by 98%.

What this paper does
Severson predicted lifetime from early-cycle data. Attia goes one step further: have ML autonomously find the optimal charging protocol itself. Bayesian optimization searches the 6-step fast-charging parameter space — automatically cycling through experiment design → test → incorporate results → next design. No human decisions between iterations. From 224 candidate protocols, it efficiently identified high-performance combinations. Result: 98% reduction in experimental time compared to conventional approaches.
Takeaway
◆ If Severson is "prediction," this is "optimization." ML starts deciding the what of experiments — not just interpreting results, but directing the next step. That's a meaningful shift in the human–AI division of labor in research.
◇ And yet the same gap remains: why this charging protocol performs better — what the electrochemical mechanism is — stays outside the model. To actually understand and improve the optimized protocol, you need mechanistic knowledge. That knowledge lives in papers, not in cycling data.
entry.summary: Bayesian optimization autonomously searched the fast-charging parameter space, cutting experimental time by 98% and identifying high-performance protocols from 224 candidates.

entry.title: Predicting Battery Lifetime Before It Declines

link.title: Predicting Battery Lifetime Before It Declines

entry.content:
Nature Energy 2019 paper ↗

Data-driven prediction of battery cycle life before capacity degradation

Trained ML on voltage curve shapes from the first 100 fast-charge cycles to predict final lifetime across a 15x range — achieving 9.1% test error and reducing what once took months of cycling to an early-stage prediction.

What this paper does
124 LFP cells were fast-charged and cycled to end-of-life. The key question: can you predict final lifetime — ranging from 150 to 2,300 cycles — from the first 100 cycles alone, before capacity visibly declines? The input is subtle: the change in the voltage discharge curve between cycle 10 and cycle 100. A feature invisible to the naked eye, but carrying early signatures of the degradation already underway. ML picked up on this. Test error: 9.1%. What used to require months of cycling to evaluate could now be predicted from early-stage data.
Takeaway
◆ The first paper to convincingly demonstrate that battery data → ML actually works at scale. The choice of input — subtle shape changes in voltage curves during cycles that look numerically fine — is the impressive part. The model is already distinguishing lifetimes in data that a human would call unremarkable.
◇ But the model doesn't explain why that voltage shape predicts lifetime — which degradation mechanism creates that signal. This is where this series begins: ML found the pattern. What caused it is a different question entirely.
entry.summary: Using only the first 100 cycles of voltage data, ML predicted final battery lifetime (150–2,300 cycles) with 9.1% test error — months before visible capacity fade.

entry.title: The Materials Project: Data Infrastructure for Materials AI

link.title: The Materials Project: Data Infrastructure for Materials AI

entry.content:
APL Materials 2013 paper ↗

Commentary: The Materials Project: A materials genome approach to accelerating materials innovation

Built a free, open database of 150,000+ inorganic materials with DFT-computed properties — the data infrastructure that underlies GNoME, the vast majority of materials ML research, and the modern materials genome initiative.

What this paper does
For AI models like GNoME to train, they need data. The Materials Project created that data. It ran high-throughput DFT simulations on tens of thousands of inorganic materials — computing crystal structure, formation energy, electronic properties, and more — and released everything as a free, open-access database. It now contains data on over 150,000 materials, and the vast majority of materials AI papers use it. The database started in 2013 made GNoME in 2023 possible.
Takeaway
◆ This is infrastructure-as-science. The Materials Project didn't produce a single novel material on its own, but it enabled an entire research field to exist. Open data accelerated the field far more than any single closed result would have — the database is a public good in the truest sense.
◇ The 10-year lag between 2013 and GNoME is a useful data point: ROI on scientific infrastructure is long-term and compounding. When designing AI systems for materials, the data layer deserves as much investment as the model architecture.
entry.summary: High-throughput DFT calculations on 150,000+ inorganic materials, freely released as an open database — the data foundation that made GNoME and most of materials AI possible.

entry.title: GNoME: Scaling Deep Learning for Materials Discovery

link.title: GNoME: Scaling Deep Learning for Materials Discovery

entry.content:
Nature 2023 paper ↗

Scaling deep learning for materials discovery

DeepMind's GNoME used GNNs trained on DFT stability data to predict stable inorganic crystal structures at scale, expanding known stable candidates from ~48,000 to ~380,000 and enabling high-throughput pre-screening before any experiment.

What this paper does
The traditional way to discover new materials is to make them in the lab — time-consuming and expensive. GNoME trains a graph neural network on DFT-computed simulation data to predict "will this combination of elements in this structure be stable?" — filtering out promising candidates at massive scale before any experiment is run. Developed by DeepMind, it expanded the known stable inorganic crystal candidate pool from ~48,000 to ~380,000 — roughly an 8x increase. Some of these have since been synthesized and confirmed experimentally. It fundamentally changed the scale and speed at which the materials search space can be explored.
Takeaway
◆ Scale is the contribution. 380,000 candidates is more than any lab could verify in a lifetime, but generating a large pool of high-probability candidates raises the hit rate of experiments dramatically. When the size of the search space changes, what's discoverable changes with it.
◇ GNoME's definition of "stable" is DFT-computed stability — which is not the same as experimentally synthesizable. The gap between computational stability and experimental synthesizability is one of the most important open problems in the field right now.
entry.summary: GNN-based GNoME expanded known stable inorganic crystal candidates from 48,000 to 380,000 — roughly 8x — with some subsequently confirmed experimentally.

entry.title: Coscientist: Autonomous Chemical Research with LLMs

link.title: Coscientist: Autonomous Chemical Research with LLMs

entry.content:
Nature 2023 paper ↗

Autonomous chemical research with large language models

GPT-4-based Coscientist searched literature, designed protocols, wrote robot control code, and executed real chemistry experiments — including Suzuki coupling — with minimal human involvement, demonstrating end-to-end autonomous research.

What this paper does
Think through the stages of chemistry research: reading papers, designing experiments, operating equipment, analyzing results. Coscientist is a system that has AI autonomously handle all of them. Given an experimental goal, GPT-4 searches relevant literature, designs a protocol, writes code to control real lab robotics, and executes it. It successfully carried out actual chemical reactions — including Suzuki coupling — with minimal human intervention. This was the first paper to demonstrate "AI actually running experiments."
Takeaway
◆ This paper makes the shift from "AI that advises" to "AI that acts" concrete. The bottleneck moves from language generation to the reliability of the physical interface — whether the robot arm actually does what the code says matters as much as AI performance. The problem is no longer just NLP; it's systems integration.
◇ The experiments are well-known reactions with established protocols. The real open challenge is novel experiments where the protocol doesn't yet exist. Integrating structure exploration with synthesis feasibility checking — the direction my Deepspace project moves toward — is a natural next step in that trajectory.
entry.summary: A GPT-4-based system autonomously conducted chemistry research end-to-end — from literature search to robotic lab execution — successfully completing Suzuki coupling with minimal human intervention.

entry.title: ChemCrow: Augmenting LLMs with Chemistry Tools

link.title: ChemCrow: Augmenting LLMs with Chemistry Tools

entry.content:
Nature Chemistry 2024 arxiv ↗

Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools

GPT-4 equipped with 18 specialized chemistry tools substantially outperformed bare GPT-4 on chemistry tasks, and successfully planned multi-step synthesis of novel compounds autonomously.

What this paper does
Ask GPT-4 chemistry questions without any scaffolding, and it often delivers wrong information with confidence. Chemistry demands precision, so this is a real problem. ChemCrow's solution: give GPT-4 18 specialized chemistry tools and let it call them as needed. Tools for molecular structure calculation, literature search, safety data lookup, synthesis pathway planning. Instead of generating answers from scratch, the model retrieves accurate information through tools and constructs its response from there. It successfully planned and autonomously executed multi-step synthesis of novel compounds.
Takeaway
◆ Tool use doesn't just improve accuracy — it changes the failure mode. GPT-4 without tools fails confidently (hallucination). ChemCrow fails more gracefully because it can cross-check its reasoning against real databases. "What tools to give the model" matters as much as "which model to use" — a framing that shapes how I think about AI system design for materials science.
◇ The choice of 18 tools encodes assumptions about the chemistry research workflow. An agent for battery electrolyte discovery would need a fundamentally different toolset. Defining that tool set — what chemical property calculators, what synthesis feasibility checks — was one of the core design decisions in my Deepspace project.
entry.summary: Connected GPT-4 to 18 specialized chemistry tools, showing that tool-augmented LLMs dramatically outperform bare LLMs on chemistry tasks — and fail more gracefully.
